one_liner: C++11 hybrid thread/fiber task scheduler from Google; tasks that block on marl primitives yield their worker instead of stalling it.
what_it_does: Marl runs lambdas on a fixed pool of worker threads via marl::schedule(), and gives fiber-aware synchronization (Event, WaitGroup, ConditionVariable, Ticket queues, defer, blocking_call). When a task waits on a marl primitive, the worker switches to another fiber or task rather than blocking the OS thread. It is a different interface from std::thread/std::async: you construct one marl::Scheduler, bind it to each thread that schedules work, and capture primitives by value.
how_it_is_fast: Per-worker task and fiber queues with work stealing (Scheduler::stealWork, random victim) and a 1 ms spin-for-work loop of nop batches before sleeping, so idle workers pick up new tasks without a kernel wake-up. Blocked tasks are parked as fibers and resumed via a hand-written register-swap routine (marl_fiber_swap in per-architecture assembly; ucontext optional via MARL_FIBERS_USE_UCONTEXT), with idle fibers pooled for reuse.
when_to_use: CPU-bound task graphs where tasks wait on each other (events, wait groups) and you want a fixed number of OS threads, e.g. SwiftShader-style rendering or shader compilation pipelines.
Many-core machines (64-128 hardware threads) where a single mutex-protected queue starts to contend; the published Windows Threadripper 3990X run shows the gap opening at 128 threads.
Cross-platform code that must run on Windows, macOS, Linux, Android, iOS, Fuchsia and Emscripten with the same scheduler.
Code that needs Go-style WaitGroup/Event semantics in C++11 without pulling in Boost or TBB.
when_not_to_use: I/O-bound servers: there is no event loop or async I/O; non-marl blocking calls (accept, std::mutex held across waits, std::condition_variable) stall a worker, and blocking_call() spawns a std::thread per call (about 17-84 us in the published runs).
Coarse-grained tasks on a few cores: the published SomeWork runs show marl within about 1-6% of a plain std::thread + std::mutex queue at 1-64 threads, so it buys little there.
New projects that need upstream fixes: the repository was archived read-only on 2026-04-27.
Workloads wanting more than 256 worker threads (MaxWorkerThreads = 256) or tiny-memory fibers: default fiber stack is 1 MiB unless changed with setFiberStackSize.
If you want stackless C++20 coroutines or a structured-concurrency API; marl is stackful and callback-based.

integration.form: static lib (CMake add_subdirectory or vcpkg; MARL_BUILD_SHARED for a shared lib)
integration.dependencies: none (googletest and google benchmark only for tests/benchmarks)
integration.min_toolchain: C++11; CI moved to clang-18 on Linux in the final commit; VS2019 CMake integration on Windows
integration.platforms: Windows, macOS, Linux, FreeBSD, Fuchsia, Emscripten, Android, iOS on arm, aarch64, loongarch64, mips64, ppc64, rv64, x86, x64
integration.thread_safety: Scheduler may be bound to any number of threads; calling marl::schedule() from an unbound thread is undefined behavior; primitives are thread-safe and should be captured by value (except ConditionVariable).

gotchas: Forgetting scheduler.unbind() before a bound thread exits makes the Scheduler destructor block forever.
Holding a std::mutex while waiting on a marl primitive can deadlock: the fiber yields with the lock held.
Multiple Scheduler instances compete for cores; README recommends one per process, and its constructor is expensive (spawns threads).
Idle workers spin for up to 1 ms before sleeping, which shows up as CPU usage on otherwise idle machines.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick marl over libco/libaco/libgo-style coroutine libraries when you want a multi-threaded work-stealing task scheduler with fiber-aware blocking primitives rather than raw context switches; pick Coros or Boost.Cobalt when you want C++20 coroutines, or minicoro/libaco when the cost of a single switch is what matters.
verified_claims_summary: The README itself has no numbers, but the gh-pages branch carries google-benchmark JSON (2020-06, release builds) for a MacBook Pro 15in 2018 (12 threads), Ubuntu and Windows 10 on a Threadripper 3990X; compiler and flags are not recorded. Against the repo's own non-marl reference executors (std::thread + std::mutex single queue, and pre-split per-thread queues) running 262144 doSomeWork tasks, marl is roughly at parity on Ubuntu (e.g. 0.293 s vs 0.297 s at 128 threads) and about 6% faster on the MacBook at 12 threads (3.35 s vs 3.55 s), but on Windows at 128 threads it takes 0.295 s vs 0.565 s single-queue and 0.651 s multi-queue (about 1.9x-2.2x, derived from page data); EventBaton task ping-pong costs about 216 ns per pass on Ubuntu, 410 ns on macOS and 635 ns on Windows (derived from page data).
status_note: Archived read-only by Google on 2026-04-27 with no 'finished' statement, but Apache-2.0, dependency-free and still packaged in vcpkg, so vendoring a pinned copy is reasonable.
